title: 1st Annual Roger Murray Lecture Series: A Conversation Between Bruce Greenwald and Tano Santos
description: A conversation with Bruce Greenwald, Robert Heilbrunn Professor Emeritus of Asset Management, and Tano Santos, David L. and M. Elsie Dodd Professor of Finance and faculty director of the Heilbrunn Center.
summary: The talk argues that sustainable value comes from companies with durable competitive advantages, such as local monopolies or specialized expertise, rather than those that attempt to diversify into unrelated areas. It contrasts modern specialized firms with legacy 'generalist' companies that lost their protected monopoly status due to globalization, resulting in diminished returns on capital. The speaker specifically advises caution on companies like Amazon and Intel that are wasting capital on poor reinvestments, while highlighting the risks of overpaying for even strong local monopolies like Deere.

claims.claim: Amazon faces tough competition in local distribution from retailers like Walmart.
claims.quote: although if they're gonna have tough time in that area competing with local walmarts and so on but that's at least an area where the network effect is reinforced by local economies of scale
claims.speaker: Bruce Greenwald

claims.claim: Google dominates the search market and is very specialized, making its core business sustainable.
claims.quote: they do search and they do search unbelievably well they focus on that narrow market that one function of the internet they completely dominate it they get better and better at because we all use google and they make a ton of money in that and that's not going away
claims.speaker: Bruce Greenwald

claims.claim: Microsoft originally specialized in operating systems but lost money when it tried to expand into other areas like Xbox.
claims.quote: microsoft originally only did operating systems and they kind of get a walmart strategy expanding at the edge of operating systems and when they decide that they're geniuses and try and do xbox they lose a lot of money
claims.speaker: Bruce Greenwald

claims.claim: Amazon is smart to understand its business has two components: a global internet interface and local distribution, which reinforces network effects.
claims.quote: i think what they've been smart enough to understand is that their business has two components one is the internet interface which is global essential but the second is local distribution and if they can get local distribution which is what they've got a ton of money on they will be fine
claims.speaker: Bruce Greenwald

claims.claim: Facebook enjoys barriers to entry associated with network externalities.
claims.quote: kind of the role of some of these big tech companies like the facebooks and the googles these companies that enjoy also some buyers to entry associated with some type of network externality in the case of facebook
claims.speaker: Tano Santos

claims.claim: Old IBM did everything unlike modern specialized tech companies.
claims.quote: if you compared to the old ibm that did everything right or the old uh you know rca going back further that did everything and general electric that did everything
claims.speaker: Bruce Greenwald

claims.claim: Old RCA did everything, implying a contrast to specialized modern companies.
claims.quote: or the old uh you know rca going back further that did everything and general electric that did everything
claims.speaker: Bruce Greenwald

claims.claim: General Motors represents the old manufacturing era of globally competitive industries.
claims.quote: manufacturing which is a big globally competitive industry natural resources which is a big globally competitive industry the axons and the general motors of the world
claims.speaker: Tano Santos

claims.claim: General Motors is cited as an example of a company that lost its monopoly status due to globalization, leading to diminished returns on capital and less value generated by growth investments.
claims.quote: so the companies like general motors like ibm that at the beginning of that period even ford have deeply entrenched protected essentially monopolies or oligopolies by the end of that period they are subject to competition
claims.speaker: Bruce Greenwald

claims.claim: IBM is mentioned alongside General Motors as a company that transitioned from a protected monopoly to facing competition, resulting in lower returns on capital.
claims.quote: so the companies like general motors like ibm that at the beginning of that period even ford have deeply entrenched protected essentially monopolies or oligopolies by the end of that period they are subject to competition
claims.speaker: Bruce Greenwald

claims.claim: Walmart's organic growth is limited because its low-income demographic faces slower income growth than the overall economy, capping future sales expansion.
claims.quote: unfortunately walmart's demographic is a low income demographic and low income demand and low income incomes are rising much less rapidly all over the world for structural reasons also related to the trend of services so that basically you know their audience or their demand is growing roughly two and a half percent less rapidly than overall
claims.speaker: Bruce Greenwald

claims.claim: Intel is wasting capital by attempting to enter driverless cars, resulting in poor returns on reinvestment.
claims.quote: if these guys are pissing it away like intel trying to get into driverless cars you can look at the acquisitions and they're basically spending a dollar for 20 cents of them which means you're going to multiply that investment number by a fifth
claims.speaker: Bruce Greenwald

claims.claim: Walmart historically generated strong returns on reinvestment by opening new stores or converting discount stores to super centers.
claims.quote: if these guys are opening new stores in their core market like walmart was for a long time you could look at the economics of a new store or the economics of a super center conversion from a discount store and you get returns on the order of one and a half two times the cost of capital
claims.speaker: Bruce Greenwald

claims.claim: Same store sales is a direct metric for organic growth at retailers like Walmart, though current growth rates may not represent the future given GDP and inflation differences.
claims.quote: so for instance for a retailer such as walmart with same store sales be a good metric of organic growth okay so you've got you've got direct measures like same store sales immature right you want to look at those but you also want to say is this current measure likely to represent the future
claims.speaker: Bruce Greenwald

claims.claim: The speaker states he will not buy Amazon at the current price.
claims.quote: on the other hand i am not going to buy it at this price
claims.speaker: Bruce Greenwald

claims.claim: The speaker views Deere as a local monopoly with robust local monopolies in agricultural equipment that has moved from manufacturing to service support.
claims.quote: the one i've talked about for years because it does indicate sort of what you're looking at is the difference between deer which has moved from a manufacturing focused company to a locally based service support company where they have local software local financing local second-hand markets and local software that runs the one runs these machines and they therefore have local monopolies
claims.speaker: Bruce Greenwald

claims.claim: The speaker states that John Deere is fully valued at this point despite its strong performance.
claims.quote: on the other hand i will now say this at this point they are fully valued yeah on the other hand there's a lot of other crap out there that's way overvalued
claims.speaker: Bruce Greenwald

claims.claim: Caterpillar is down since the beginning of the year and does not understand the local monopoly dynamics of the agricultural equipment sector.
claims.quote: caterpillar which doesn't understand that is actually down since the beginning of the year so i think it's literally there are a lot of unexploited opportunities like that uh that are out there
claims.speaker: Bruce Greenwald

claims.claim: Caterpillar failed miserably in an attempt to enter the US farm equipment business by partnering with a German company.
claims.quote: it's uh you know a caterpillar tried they if i remember correctly they partnered up with the german farm equipment company class in marketing uh a combine that they wanted to introduce and compete for the u.s farm equipment business and they fell miserably
claims.speaker: Bruce Greenwald
